# The scenario

The Georgia Department of Community Supervision is considering a risk model to guide parole decisions. Every person released to parole would get a predicted probability of being **rearrested within three years**. The department has two proposed uses:

- **Use A:** people above a threshold get **more restrictive supervision** (more check-ins, electronic monitoring, faster revocation).
- **Use B:** people above a threshold get **priority for reentry services** (housing assistance, job placement, a case manager).

The department has promised that the model **will not use race**. You've been hired to build it and to tell them whether that promise means what they think it means.

**What you're turning in:** this rendered document, published in the `assignments/` folder of your portfolio.

**How this assignment works:** it has less scaffolding than earlier ones. The **Week 11 lab** (COMPAS) is your fully worked example: almost every step here has a matching step there. Where the NIJ data behaves differently from COMPAS, the instructions below tell you. Everywhere else, adapt the lab code yourself.

| A5 part | Week 11 lab step |
|---|---|
| 3.1 odds ratios | Step 3 |
| 4.1 predictions + confusion matrix | Steps 4–5 |
| 4.3 threshold sweep | Step 5 (`rates_at()`) |
| 4.4 ROC + AUC | Step 6 |
| 5.1–5.2 errors by race | Step 7 |
| 5.3 what carries race in | Step 8 |

Two differences from the lab: the outcome is called **`recid`** (not `two_year_recid`), and you **fit on `train` and evaluate on `test`**. In the lab we fit and scored on the same data. So every `predict()` in Parts 4 and 5 needs `newdata = test`.


# The data

The National Institute of Justice's **Recidivism Forecasting Challenge** data: 25,835 people released from Georgia prisons to parole supervision, 2013–2015. Download the CSV from Canvas, put it in your portfolio's `data/` folder, and rename it `nij_recidivism.csv`.

A few things to know before you start:

- **Race is recorded only as Black or white.** The data includes no one else.
- **Counts are top-coded:** "10 or more" prior felony arrests is stored as text. `parse_number()` turns it into 10, which undercounts people with many more.
- **`Residence_PUMA`** is not a census PUMA code. NIJ grouped Georgia's PUMAs into 25 areas and numbered them 1–25 to protect privacy. You can use it to group people by place, but you can't map it.
- **`Training_Sample`** is NIJ's own train/test split. Use it.

# Part 1: Load and clean


```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)

to01 <- function(x) {
  x <- toupper(trimws(as.character(x)))
  case_when(x %in% c("TRUE", "T", "YES", "Y", "1")  ~ 1L,
            x %in% c("FALSE", "F", "NO", "N", "0") ~ 0L,
            TRUE ~ NA_integer_)
}

nij <- read_csv("assignments/data/nij_recidivism.csv") %>%
  mutate(
    recid              = to01(Recidivism_Within_3years),
    male               = as.integer(Gender == "M"),
    age_group          = factor(Age_at_Release),
    prison_years       = factor(Prison_Years,
                                levels = c("Less than 1 year", "1-2 years",
                                           "Greater than 2 to 3 years",
                                           "More than 3 years")),
    prior_fel_arrests  = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony),
    prior_misd_arrests = parse_number(Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd),
    puma               = factor(Residence_PUMA)
  )

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)
```

**1.1** How many people are in `train` and in `test`? What share of each was rearrested within three years?

```{r}
nij %>%
  mutate(set = if_else(Training_Sample == 1, "train", "test")) %>%
  group_by(set) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            share_rearrested = mean(recid))
```

*"train" has 18,028 observations and test has 7807. Respectively, the share rearrested within three years was around 0.58 and 0.57.*

**1.2** Look at `Gang_Affiliated`. How many values are missing, and who are they? (Hint: cross-tabulate it with `Gender`.) What would happen to your sample if you added this variable to a model without handling the missing values?

```{r}
nij %>% count(Gender, Gang_Affiliated)

sum(is.na(nij$Gang_Affiliated))
```

*There are 3,167 missing values and each one falls into the women's category. No women in the data have a value assigned and it appears that gang affiliation has been recorded for men only. If I were to add Gang_Affiliated to my model, R would drop all 3,167 women and the model would be trained on men alone. It would stop scoring women at all and every accuracy number should be understood as relating to the men in the dataset. *

# Part 2: What would you know at the moment of decision?

The parole decision happens **at release**. Some columns in this file were recorded **during** the three years of supervision that followed.

**2.1** Sort every predictor column into one of two lists. You don't need code; use `names(nij)` and the column names.

Known at release:
`Gender`, `Race`, `Age_at_Release`, `Residence_PUMA`, `Gang_Affiliated`, `Supervision_Risk_Score_First`, `Supervision_Level_First`, `Education_Level`, `Dependents`, `Prison_Offense`, `Prison_Years`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Felony`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Misd`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Violent`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Property`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_Drug`, `_v1` (prior parole/probation violation arrests), `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_DVCharges`, `Prior_Arrest_Episodes_GunCharges`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Felony`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Misd`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Viol`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Prop`, `Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Drug`, `_v2` (prior parole/probation violation convictions), `_v3` (prior domestic violence convictions), `_v4` (prior gun convictions), `Prior_Revocations_Parole`, `Prior_Revocations_Probation`, `Condition_MH_SA`, `Condition_Cog_Ed`, `Condition_Other`

Recorded during supervision (leakage):
`Violations_ElectronicMonitoring`, `Violations_Instruction`, `Violations_FailToReport`, `Violations_MoveWithoutPermission`, `Delinquency_Reports`, `Program_Attendances`, `Program_UnexcusedAbsences`, `Residence_Changes`, `Avg_Days_per_DrugTest`, `DrugTests_THC_Positive`, `DrugTests_Cocaine_Positive`, `DrugTests_Meth_Positive`, `DrugTests_Other_Positive`, `Percent_Days_Employed`, `Jobs_Per_Year`, `Employment_Exempt`, `Recidivism_Arrest_Year1`, `Recidivism_Arrest_Year2`, `Recidivism_Arrest_Year3`


**2.2** Pick one variable from the right-hand column and explain, in two sentences, why including it would make your model look better than it really is. 

Violations_FailToReport records missed check-ins during the three years of supervision which could mean someone has already been arrested or jailed somewhere else. The model would be reading an early record of the outcome and calling it a prediction, so someone who hasn't missed a check-in because they were just released would impact the actual accuracy.

# Part 3: Build a race-blind model

Start from this model.

```{r}
#| label: base-model
base_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                  prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests,
                family = binomial,
                data = train)

summary(base_fit)
```

**3.1** Exponentiate the coefficients. Interpret the odds ratio for `prior_fel_arrests` in one sentence, using the word *odds* correctly.

```{r}
tibble(
  term       = names(coef(base_fit)),
  odds_ratio = exp(coef(base_fit)),
  ci_low     = exp(confint.default(base_fit)[, 1]),
  ci_high    = exp(confint.default(base_fit)[, 2])
) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

*Holding sex, age, time served, and misdemeanor arrests constant, each additional prior felony arrest multiplies a person's odds of rearrest within three years by 1.18, about 18% higher odds per arrest. Since the count is top-coded at 10, "one more arrest" begins to stop holding meaning.*

**3.2** Constant on the odds, not on the probability. Use `predict(..., type = "response")` with `newdata` to compute the predicted probability for two made-up people, then add one prior felony arrest to each:

- a man, age 23–27, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest
- a man, age 48 or older, 1–2 years in prison, 2 prior felony arrests, 1 misdemeanor arrest

How much does one more arrest change each person's probability? Why are the two changes different?

```{r}
people <- tibble(
  male               = c(1, 1),
  age_group          = factor(c("23-27", "48 or older"), levels = levels(nij$age_group)),
  prison_years       = factor(c("1-2 years", "1-2 years"), levels = levels(nij$prison_years)),
  prior_fel_arrests  = c(2, 2),
  prior_misd_arrests = c(1, 1)
)

p_before <- predict(base_fit, newdata = people, type = "response")

p_after <- predict(base_fit,
                   newdata = people %>% mutate(prior_fel_arrests = prior_fel_arrests + 1),
                   type = "response")

tibble(person   = c("Age 23-27", "Age 48+"),
       p_before = round(p_before, 3),
       p_after  = round(p_after, 3),
       change_pts = round((p_after - p_before) * 100, 1))
```

*One more prior felony arrest raises the 23–27-year-old's predicted probability from 56.4% to 60.5%. It raises the man 48 or older from 17.9% to 20.4%. In both cases the odds are multiplied by the same 1.18 and the probabilities move by different amounts along the logistic curve. Younger men start close to the middle, where a push to the odds moves the probability a lot. And, the older men start low on the flat part of the curve, where it's felt less.*

**3.3** Improve the model. Add at least **three** predictors from your "known at release" list. Keep race out. Call it `my_fit`. In two or three sentences, say what you added and why you expected each one to help.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check for missing values before you add a variable
Some columns have blanks: `Prison_Offense` is missing for about 1 in 8 people, and `Supervision_Level_First` for about 1 in 15. If you add one as it is, `glm()` **silently drops** those people from training, and `predict()` returns `NA` for them in `test`. Then `mean()` gives `NA` in Parts 4–6, and `table()` quietly leaves them out. Either leave the variable out, or keep the blanks as their own category, for example `mutate(offense = replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing"))`. Whichever you choose, say so in your answer.
:::

```{r}
#| label: my-model
to_num <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  case_when(x == "Yes" ~ 1,
            x == "No"  ~ 0,
            TRUE       ~ suppressWarnings(parse_number(x)))
}

conv_cols <- c("Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Felony", "Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Misd",
               "Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Viol",   "Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Prop",
               "Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Drug",   "_v2", "_v3", "_v4")

nij <- nij %>%
  mutate(
    offense    = factor(replace_na(Prison_Offense, "Missing")),
    education  = factor(Education_Level),
    dependents = parse_number(as.character(Dependents)),
    across(all_of(conv_cols), to_num, .names = "conv_{.col}")
  ) %>%
  rename(conv_ppviol = `conv__v2`, conv_dv = `conv__v3`, conv_gun = `conv__v4`)

train <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 1)
test  <- nij %>% filter(Training_Sample == 0)

train %>%
  summarize(across(c(offense, education, dependents, starts_with("conv_")),
                   ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_missing")

my_fit <- glm(recid ~ male + age_group + prison_years +
                prior_fel_arrests + prior_misd_arrests +
                education + offense + dependents +
                conv_Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Felony + conv_Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Misd +
                conv_Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Viol   + conv_Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Prop +
                conv_Prior_Conviction_Episodes_Drug   +
                conv_ppviol + conv_dv + conv_gun,
              family = binomial,
              data = train)

summary(my_fit)

c(base = AIC(base_fit), mine = AIC(my_fit))
```

*I added education level, prison offense, number of dependents, and all eight prior-conviction measures. I expected education and dependents to capture a person's footing at release (employability and people depending on them), prison offense to capture what sent them to prison this time, and convictions to record a charge that held up in court. Prison_Offense is blank for about 1 in 8 people, so I kept the blanks as their own "Missing" category instead of letting glm() drop them, and the model trained on all 18,028 people. AIC fell from 21,966 to 21,840, but the effects varied. Prior misdemeanor, violent, and property convictions mattered, while felony and drug convictions added almost nothing once felony arrests were already in the model, and dependents had no detectable effect.*

# Part 4: Choosing a threshold

**4.1** Add a column `p_hat` to `test` with predicted probabilities from `my_fit`, and a column `pred_50` that flags anyone at or above 0.5. (Parts 5 and 6 use these column names.) Then make a confusion matrix and compute sensitivity and specificity.

```{r}
test <- test %>%
  mutate(p_hat   = predict(my_fit, newdata = test, type = "response"),
         pred_50 = as.integer(p_hat >= 0.5))

sum(is.na(test$p_hat))

table(Predicted = test$pred_50, Actual = test$recid)

test %>%
  summarize(
    sensitivity = sum(pred_50 == 1 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
    specificity = sum(pred_50 == 0 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0)
  )
```

*At a threshold of 0.5, the model correctly flags 3,669 of the 4,483 people who were rearrested, a sensitivity of 81.8%, and misses the other 814. It does much worse on people who stayed out of trouble: it leaves only 1,549 of 3,324 unflagged, a specificity of 46.6%. The other 1,775 people, more than half of everyone who was not rearrested, are labeled high risk anyway. At 0.5 the model leans hard toward flagging people.*

**4.2** What share of the test set does your model label "high risk" at 0.5? Compare it to the share actually rearrested. What does that tell you about 0.5 as a default for this data?

*At 0.5, the model labels 69.7% of the test set high risk, but only 57.4% were actually rearrested, so it flags about 12 percentage points more people than there are rearrests. Because more than half of this population was rearrested, most people's predicted probability sits above 0.5, and a "high risk" label at that cutoff describes most of the caseload instead of singling anyone out. 0.5 is a default, but the threshold should be set by what each kind of mistake costs.*

**4.3** Compute sensitivity and specificity for every threshold from 0.30 to 0.80 in steps of 0.05, and plot both lines on one chart with threshold on the x-axis.

Hint: in the lab you called `rates_at()` three times by hand. Here you need eleven thresholds. `map_dfr(thresholds, function(t) ...)` runs the same code once per threshold and stacks the results into one data frame. Your version will need `p_hat` instead of `pred`, and `recid` instead of `two_year_recid`.

```{r}
rates_at <- function(t) {
  flag <- as.integer(test$p_hat >= t)
  tibble(threshold     = t,
         sensitivity   = sum(flag == 1 & test$recid == 1) / sum(test$recid == 1),
         specificity   = sum(flag == 0 & test$recid == 0) / sum(test$recid == 0),
         share_flagged = mean(flag))
}

thresholds <- seq(0.30, 0.80, by = 0.05)
sweep <- map_dfr(thresholds, rates_at)

sweep %>% mutate(across(-threshold, ~ round(.x, 3)))

sweep %>%
  pivot_longer(c(sensitivity, specificity), names_to = "rate", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(threshold, value, color = rate)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = thresholds) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(sensitivity = "#c0392b", specificity = "#2c3e50")) +
  labs(x = "Threshold", y = NULL, color = NULL,
       title = "Raising the threshold trades sensitivity for specificity",
       subtitle = "my_fit on the NIJ test set") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

**4.4** Plot the ROC curve for `my_fit` on the test set with `pROC` and report the AUC. In one sentence: what does the AUC tell you, and what doesn't it tell you about the decision the department has to make?

```{r}
library(pROC)

roc_obj <- roc(test$recid, test$p_hat, quiet = TRUE)
auc(roc_obj)

plot(roc_obj, legacy.axes = TRUE, print.auc = TRUE,
     main = "ROC curve, my_fit on the test set")
```

*An AUC of 0.707 means that if you pick one person who was rearrested and one who wasn't, the model gives the rearrested person the higher score about 71% of the time. It doesn't tell you what a wrong flag costs someone or whether the mistakes are equally examined between Black and white parolees.*

# Part 5: Is it race-blind?

Race isn't in your model. Now check the errors by race on the **test set**.

**5.1** At the threshold of 0.5, compute for each race: the share labeled high risk, the share actually rearrested, the **false positive rate** (labeled high risk, not rearrested, out of everyone not rearrested), and the **false negative rate**.

```{r}
race_errors <- function(t, data = test) {
  data %>%
    mutate(flag = as.integer(p_hat >= t)) %>%
    group_by(Race) %>%
    summarize(threshold        = t,
              n                = n(),
              share_flagged    = mean(flag),
              share_rearrested = mean(recid),
              fpr = sum(flag == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0),
              fnr = sum(flag == 0 & recid == 1) / sum(recid == 1),
              .groups = "drop")
}

race_errors(0.5) %>% mutate(across(share_flagged:fnr, ~ round(.x, 3)))
```

**5.2** Repeat 5.1 at two other thresholds from your sweep. Does the gap between groups close, stay, or flip?

```{r}
by_threshold <- bind_rows(race_errors(0.40), race_errors(0.50), race_errors(0.65))

by_threshold %>% mutate(across(share_flagged:fnr, ~ round(.x, 3)))

by_threshold %>%
  select(Race, threshold, fpr, fnr) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Race, values_from = c(fpr, fnr)) %>%
  mutate(fpr_gap_pts = round(100 * (fpr_BLACK - fpr_WHITE), 1),
         fnr_gap_pts = round(100 * (fnr_BLACK - fnr_WHITE), 1))
```

*At 0.40, Black parolees who were not rearrested are wrongly flagged 73.9% of the time against 62.2% for white parolees. At 0.50 the gap is 10.6 points (57.9% vs. 47.4%). At 0.65 it shrinks to 3.1 points (27.0% vs. 23.9%). Much of that narrowing happens because everyone's false positive rate falls as the threshold rises, so there's less room for a gap. The gap narrows as the threshold rises, but it never closes or flips.*

*A Black parolee who does not reoffend is about 13% more likely to be wrongly flagged at 0.65 than a white one, compared with about 22% more likely at 0.50. White parolees who were rearrested are consistently the ones more likely to be missed. Moving the threshold changes how big the disparity is but doesn't account for which group.*

**5.3** Investigate at least two candidates by comparing their distributions by race. Possibilities include age, prior arrests, prison offense, and place (`puma`). Show your evidence with a table or chart for each.

```{r}
# prior felony arrests + mean predicted score
test %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  summarize(mean_fel_arrests = mean(prior_fel_arrests),
            share_10_plus    = mean(prior_fel_arrests >= 10),
            mean_misd_arrests = mean(prior_misd_arrests),
            mean_p_hat       = mean(p_hat))

ggplot(test, aes(prior_fel_arrests, fill = Race)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(prop)), position = "dodge") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10, labels = c(0:9, "10+")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(BLACK = "#8e44ad", WHITE = "#e67e22")) +
  labs(x = "Prior felony arrests", y = "Share of group", fill = NULL,
       title = "Prior felony arrests by race (test set)") +
  theme_minimal()

# age at release
test %>%
  count(Race, age_group) %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3)) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Race, values_from = share)

# place: share Black in each PUMA group
puma_race <- nij %>%
  group_by(puma) %>%
  summarize(n = n(), share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"))

range(puma_race$share_black)

ggplot(puma_race, aes(reorder(puma, share_black), share_black)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(nij$Race == "BLACK"), linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "PUMA group", y = "Share Black",
       title = "Share of parolees who are Black, by PUMA group",
       subtitle = "Dashed line = statewide share") +
  theme_minimal()

# prison offense
test %>%
  count(Race, offense) %>%
  group_by(Race) %>%
  mutate(share = round(n / sum(n), 3)) %>%
  select(-n) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Race, values_from = share)
```

*I compared prior arrests, age, prison offense, and place by race. White parolees in the test set average slightly more prior felony arrests than Black parolees (5.84 vs. 5.70) and more misdemeanor arrests (3.55 vs. 3.16), and the share top-coded at 10 or more is nearly identical (22.8% vs. 24.0%). There are interesting results with age. 32.6% of Black parolees are under 28 at release, compared with 21.2% of white parolees, and age is the strongest predictor in my model. The oldest group has about one-tenth the odds of rearrest of the youngest. Because the model gives every young person a high score, the young Black parolees who did not reoffend get flagged along with those who did, and there are more of them. The results suggest Black parolees are more often in prison for violent non-sex offenses (26.2% vs. 14.9%), which raises their scores slightly, while white parolees are more often in for property offenses (36.6% vs. 28.5%), which raises theirs more. Place is the strongest proxy of all, since the share of parolees who are Black ranges from 15% to 88% across PUMA groups, but it isn't in my model yet. The result is that Black parolees end up with a higher average predicted probability (59.2% vs. 56.2%) even though their actual rearrest rates differ by less than two points.*


# Part 6: Does it hold up in places it hasn't seen?

Use leave-one-PUMA-group-out cross-validation **on the training set**, the same recipe as Week 10's leave-one-district-out.

```{r}
pumas <- levels(train$puma)

cv_puma <- map_dfr(pumas, function(u) {
  cv_train <- train %>% filter(puma != u)
  cv_test  <- train %>% filter(puma == u)

  fit <- glm(formula(my_fit), family = binomial, data = cv_train)

  cv_test %>%
    mutate(pred = as.integer(predict(fit, newdata = cv_test,
                                     type = "response") >= 0.5)) %>%
    summarize(puma       = u,
              n          = n(),
              share_black = mean(Race == "BLACK"),
              accuracy   = mean(pred == recid),
              fpr        = sum(pred == 1 & recid == 0) / sum(recid == 0))
})
```

**6.1** Plot each PUMA group's false positive rate against its share of Black parolees. What pattern, if any, do you see?

```{r}
cor(cv_puma$share_black, cv_puma$fpr)

ggplot(cv_puma, aes(share_black, fpr)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "grey50", fill = "grey85") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "#8e44ad", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = puma), size = 3, vjust = -1.1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of parolees who are Black",
       y = "False positive rate (held-out PUMA group)",
       size = "Parolees",
       title = "Leave-one-PUMA-out false positive rates") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*There is a modest upward pattern with a correlation 0.41. PUMA groups where more of the parolees are Black tend to have higher false positive rates, from about 49% at the low end of the fitted line to about 55% at the high end. The pattern is weak and leans heavily 17 and 24, the two least-Black areas at about 15%, have by far the lowest false positive rates (about 42%), and without them the trend is close to flat. Most of the variation sits among places with similar racial makeup. Groups 16, 25, 14, 7, 1, and 10 all have false positive rates near 57–59% despite ranging from 29% to 72% Black.*

**6.2** If you put `puma` itself into the model as a predictor, would that make the model more or less race-blind? Make an argument using what you found in 6.1. (You may test it, but you don't have to.)

*Adding puma would make the model less race-blind. The share of parolees who are Black ranges from 15% to 88% across the 25 PUMA groups, so giving each place its own coefficient lets the model assume some people are riskier than others and then charge everyone from there. Part 6.1 suggests place and the model's errors already move together and it might even raise accuracy, since places differ in rearrest rates. However, part of what those place differences reflect is where police patrol and make arrests, and it would mean a parolee's supervision depends partly on their address.*

# Part 7: The memo

Write a memo (**400–600 words**) to the Department of Community Supervision. 

Dear Deputy Commissioner, 

I have built a model that estimates each parolee's chance of being rearrested within three years. It uses only what the department knows on the day of release: age, sex, time served, prior arrests and convictions, the offense that led to prison, education, and number of dependents. It does not use race, and I tested it on 7,807 people it had never seen. Given one person who was rearrested and one who was not, it ranks the rearrested person higher about 71% of the time. For applications like this, that means the model will be wrong about a portion of people, but there are nuances to the mistakes and use cases. 

A false positive is a person the model calls high risk who in fact stays out of trouble. A false negative is a person the model calls low risk who is later rearrested.

Use A, restrictive supervision: threshold 0.65. A false positive here can be an expensive mistake, leading to extra check-ins and monitoring, and that extra scrutiny can itself create the violation that sends them back. A false negative still gets standard supervision. At 0.65, the model flags 42% of parolees, and 26% of the people who stayed out of trouble are flagged anyway. At the default cutoff of 0.50, that figure is 53%. More than half of the people who did nothing wrong would be put under tighter control. The drawback of 0.65 is that it catches only 54% of the people who are rearrested. 

Use B, priority for reentry services: threshold 0.40. Here, the costs flip. Giving housing help or a case manager to someone who would have been fine costs a service slot but missing someone who needed help is the expensive mistake. At 0.40, the model catches 91% of the people who are later rearrested. It also flags 82% of everyone, so if the department has fewer slots than that, it should use the score to decide who goes first.

Leaving race out does not mean equal treatment. Black and white parolees in the test group were rearrested at nearly the same rate, 58% and 56%. The model still treats them differently. At 0.50, it wrongly flags 58% of Black parolees who stayed out of trouble, compared with 47% of white parolees. At 0.65 the gap narrows to 27% versus 24%, but at no threshold I tested did it close or reverse. Meanwhile, white parolees who did reoffend are the ones more likely to be missed.

My findings suggest a main reason is age. Youth is the strongest predictor in the model, and 33% of Black parolees are under 28 at release, compared with 21% of white parolees. The model scores young people as high risk, so young Black parolees who have not offended would be grouped with those who do. 

For Use B, an uneven error rate means one group is offered help more often. For Use A, it means one group is punished more often for something its members did not do.

I would not deploy this for Use A, unless a supervising officer can review every flag and override it. The department should also disclose the wrongful-flag rate for Black and white parolees every year.
